# Himalayan Climbing Expeditions

The data this week comes from [The Himalayan Database](https://www.himalayandatabase.com/).

>The Himalayan Database is a compilation of records for all expeditions that have climbed in the Nepal Himalaya. The database is based on the expedition archives of Elizabeth Hawley, a longtime journalist based in Kathmandu, and it is supplemented by information gathered from books, alpine journals and correspondence with Himalayan climbers.
>
>The data cover all expeditions from 1905 through Spring 2019 to more than 465 significant peaks in Nepal. Also included are expeditions to both sides of border peaks such as Everest, Cho Oyu, Makalu and Kangchenjunga as well as to some smaller border peaks. Data on expeditions to trekking peaks are included for early attempts, first ascents and major accidents.

h/t to [Alex Cookson](https://twitter.com/alexcookson) for sharing and cleaning this data!

This [blog post](https://www.alexcookson.com/post/analyzing-himalayan-peaks-first-ascents/) by [Alex Cookson](https://twitter.com/alexcookson) explores the data in greater detail.

I don't want to underplay that there are some positives and some awful negatives for native Sherpa climbers. [One-third of Everest deaths are Sherpa Climbers](https://www.npr.org/sections/parallels/2018/04/14/599417489/one-third-of-everest-deaths-are-sherpa-climbers).  

Also National Geographic has [5 Ways to help the Sherpas of Everest](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/news/2014/4/140424-sherpas-avalanche-help-donations/).

### Get the data here

```r
# Get the Data

# Read in with tidytuesdayR package 
# Install from CRAN via: install.packages("tidytuesdayR")
# This loads the readme and all the datasets for the week of interest

# Either ISO-8601 date or year/week works!

tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load('2020-09-22')
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load(2020, week = 39)

climbers <- tuesdata$climbers

# Or read in the data manually

members <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-09-22/members.csv')
expeditions <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-09-22/expeditions.csv')
peaks <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-09-22/peaks.csv')
```
# Data Dictionary

### `peaks.csv`

| variable                   | class     | description                                                  |
| :------------------------- | :-------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |
| peak_id                    | character | Unique identifier for peak                                   |
| peak_name                  | character | Common name of peak                                          |
| peak_alternative_name      | character | Alternative name of peak (for example, the "Mount Everest" is "Sagarmatha" in Nepalese) |
| height_metres              | double    | Height of peak in metres                                     |
| climbing_status            | character | Whether the peak has been climbed                            |
| first_ascent_year          | double    | Year of first successful ascent, if applicable               |
| first_ascent_country       | character | Country name(s) of expedition members part of the first ascent. Can have multiple values if members were from different countries. Country name is as of date of ascent (for example, "W Germany" for ascents before 1990). |
| first_ascent_expedition_id | character | Unique identifier for expedition. Can be linked to `expeditions` or `members` tables. |



### `expeditions.csv`

| variable           | class     | description                                                  |
| :----------------- | :-------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |
| expedition_id      | character | Unique identifier for expedition. Can be linked to `peaks` or `members` tables. |
| peak_id            | character | Unique identifier for peak. Can be linked to `peaks` table.  |
| peak_name          | character | Common name for peak                                         |
| year               | double    | Year of expedition                                           |
| season             | character | Season of expedition (Spring, Summer, etc.)                  |
| basecamp_date      | date      | Date of expedition arrival at basecamp                       |
| highpoint_date        | date      | Date of expedition summiting the peak for the first time or, if peak wasn't reached, date of reaching its highpoint |
| termination_date   | date      | Date the expedition was terminated                           |
| termination_reason | character | Primary reason the expedition was terminated. There are two possibilities for a successful expeditions, depending on whether the main peak or a sub-peak was summitted. |
| highpoint_metres   | double    | Elevation highpoint of the expedition                        |
| members            | double    | Number of expedition members. For expeditions in Nepal, this is usually the number of foreigners listed on the expedition permit. For expeditions in China, this is usually the number of non-hired members. |
| member_deaths      | double    | Number of expeditions members who died                       |
| hired_staff        | double    | Number of hired staff who went above basecamp                |
| hired_staff_deaths | double    | Number of hired staff who died                               |
| oxygen_used        | logical   | Whether oxygen was used by at least one member of the expedition |
| trekking_agency    | character | Name of the trekking agency                                  |



### `members.csv`

| variable             | class     | description                                                  |
| :------------------- | :-------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |

| citizenship          | character | Citizenship of the person                                    |

| hired                | logical   | Whether the person was hired by the expedition               |
| highpoint_metres     | double    | Elevation highpoint of the person                            |
| success              | logical   | Whether the person was successful in summitting a main peak or sub-peak, depending on the goal of expedition |
| solo                 | logical   | Whether the person attempted a solo ascent                   |
| oxygen_used          | logical   | Whether the person used oxygen                               |
| died                 | logical   | Whether the person died                                      |
| death_cause          | character | Primary cause of death                                       |
| death_height_metres  | double    | Height at which the person died                              |
| injured              | logical   | Whether the person was injured                               |

| injury_height_metres | double    | Height at which the injury occurred                          |


### Cleaning Script

```r
# Libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)


# Peaks
peaks <- read_csv("./himalayan-expeditions/raw/peaks.csv") %>%
  transmute(
    peak_id = PEAKID,
    peak_name = PKNAME,
    peak_alternative_name = PKNAME2,
    height_metres = HEIGHTM,
    climbing_status = PSTATUS,
    first_ascent_year = PYEAR,
    first_ascent_country = PCOUNTRY,
    first_ascent_expedition_id = PEXPID

    climbing_status = case_when(
      climbing_status == 0 ~ "Unknown",
      climbing_status == 1 ~ "Unclimbed",
      climbing_status == 2 ~ "Climbed"
    )
  )

# Create small dataframe of peak names to join to other dataframes

# Expeditions

  left_join(peak_names, by = c("PEAKID" = "peak_id")) %>%
  transmute(
    expedition_id = EXPID,
    peak_id = PEAKID,
    peak_name,
    year = YEAR,
    season = SEASON,
    basecamp_date = BCDATE,

# Has Everest become safer?

**Yes, a lot, but the biggest gains went to the people who carry the risk for everyone else, and those gains have stalled.**

*Source: Himalayan Database, Everest (peak EVER) records for 1950–2019, 21,813 team-member entries. Code and tables are in `outputs/everest-safety/`.*

![Everest death rate by decade](everest-safety/death_rate_by_decade.png)

## Two kinds of climbers

The data separates **expedition members**, who are the paying or permit-holding climbers, from **hired staff**. Hired staff are mostly Sherpa and other high-altitude workers who fix ropes, carry loads and guide. The measure used here is deaths per 1,000 people listed on Everest teams. One person on two expeditions counts twice, so this is closer to risk per expedition than risk per lifetime.

## 1. Before 1990: the staff took the heaviest risk

Between 1950 and 1989, **about 1 in 6 hired staff on the mountain died (157 per 1,000)**, against about 1 in 50 expedition members (20 per 1,000). In the 1970s the staff rate peaked at 365 per 1,000, but that is only 52 people and 19 deaths, so treat it as rough.

## 2. Since 1990: both rates fell, staff far more

| Era | Expedition members | Hired staff |
|---|---|---|
| 1950–1989 | 19.8 per 1,000 (54 deaths) | 157.3 per 1,000 (42 deaths) |
| 1990–2019 | 10.4 per 1,000 (128 deaths) | 10.7 per 1,000 (68 deaths) |

- Member risk **roughly halved**. Staff risk fell about **15-fold**. Both drops are statistically clear (p < 0.001).
- In the commercial era the two groups carry about the same risk (10.4 vs 10.7 per 1,000, no meaningful difference).
- The mountain has also become far more crowded. Team entries were 2,988 in 1950–1989 and 18,653 in 1990–2019, so total deaths rose even as the rate fell.

## 3. What changed

Summit success went up, and **oxygen use rose in step with it**:

- Among expedition members, the summit rate rose from 7% in the 1980s to 52% in the 2010s.
- The share using bottled oxygen rose from 19% to 62% over the same period.

These match the commercial era's guided, supported climbs, but this data cannot prove what caused the safer outcomes. The data does not record fixed ropes, weather forecasting or guide experience.

## 4. Progress has stalled, and disasters hit staff hardest

Hired-staff deaths per 1,000 by five-year period:

| Years | 1990–94 | 1995–99 | 2000–04 | 2005–09 | 2010–14 | 2015–19 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Staff | 46.9 | 28.9 | 3.2 | 5.1 | **15.0** | 7.1 |
| Members | 10.2 | 19.1 | 10.0 | 9.4 | 7.8 | 9.5 |

- Staff risk was at its lowest in the 2000s, then rose again in 2010–14.
- Two events drive this. **2014** (an avalanche in the Khumbu Icefall) killed 17 staff and no members. **2015** (the Nepal earthquake) killed 11 staff and 3 members.
- Without those two years, the 1990–2019 staff rate is **6.8 per 1,000**, against 11.0 for members. That is lower than the members' rate.
- Across the individual years since 1990, there is no statistically clear downward trend for either group. The big drop happened around the turn of the millennium, and since then rates have been flat at about 5–15 per 1,000.

**Causes differ by group** (deaths since 1990):

| Group | Leading causes |
|---|---|
| Hired staff | Avalanche 33 of 68, fall 8 |
| Expedition members | Fall 31, altitude sickness 24, exhaustion 23 |

Staff are lost mostly to mountain hazards they cannot avoid, such as avalanches in the Icefall. Members die more from altitude and exhaustion.

## Bottom line

Everest is safer than it was. A typical climber's risk of dying on a trip is about half what it was before 1990, and for staff it is a small fraction of what it was. But a rate of about 10 deaths per 1,000 is not low, and since 2000 it has stopped improving. Each additional crowded season adds to the number of people exposed to avalanches.

## Caveats

- **Observational data.** These are associations, not proof of what made the mountain safer.
- **Counting people.** The member table lists 6,730 hired-staff entries for Everest, but the expedition table reports 12,741 hired staff above base camp. The member table may therefore miss many staff, and the rate depends on which were recorded. Deaths match exactly (186 members, 120 staff in both tables).
- **Hired-staff numbers before 1990 are small** (267 entries), so those rates are imprecise. See the confidence intervals in `by_decade.csv`.
- **Deaths per summit** (an alternative denominator) gives a similar picture, in `by_era.csv`.
- The records run to spring 2019, so the COVID years and later are not covered. The data shows what was recorded, and unrecorded deaths and early-era gaps are possible.

result:
**Everest has become safer, but most of the improvement came before 2000.** The data runs from 1950 to spring 2019. The deaths are in `data/members.csv` and `data/expeditions.csv`. The story is in `outputs/story.md`, with the chart and supporting tables in `outputs/everest-safety/`.

| Deaths per 1,000 people on Everest teams | 1950–1989 | 1990–2019 |
|---|---|---|
| Expedition members | 19.8 | 10.4 |
| Hired staff | 157.3 | 10.7 |

- **Members:** their death rate roughly halved. The drop is statistically clear (p < 0.001).
- **Hired staff:** their rate fell about 15-fold, from about 1 in 6 before 1990 to about 1 in 100 since.
- **Commercial era:** staff and members now face about the same risk. Summit success and bottled-oxygen use rose together, but I can't show which caused the safer outcomes.
- **Stalled since 2000:** the rate has been flat at roughly 5–15 per 1,000 since the early 2000s. Individual years show no clear downward trend for either group.
- **2014 and 2015:** these two years hit staff hardest. Staff deaths were 17 in the 2014 icefall avalanche and 11 in the 2015 earthquake. Without those two years, the staff rate since 1990 is 6.8 per 1,000, below the members' 11.0.
- **Causes of death:** since 1990, avalanches caused 33 of the 68 staff deaths. Members die more from falls, altitude sickness and exhaustion.

**Method:**
- **Rate:** deaths divided by team-member entries on Everest, counting a person once per expedition.
- **Groups:** the `hired` flag separates members from staff.
- **Confidence intervals:** Wilson intervals around each rate.
- **Tests:** Fisher exact tests for the before/after comparisons and Spearman correlation for the yearly trend.

**Caveats:**
- **Possible undercount of staff:** `members.csv` lists 6,730 hired-staff entries for Everest, but `expeditions.csv` reports 12,741 hired staff above base camp, so staff may be undercounted there. Death totals are the same in both files.
- **Small early samples:** the pre-1990 staff numbers are small (267 entries), so those rates are imprecise.
- **Association only:** this is observational data, so it shows association, not cause.
- **Not run:** I didn't run the separate QA step.
